• **DAV Academic Standard**: Official Class 7 English Practice Book Chapter 7 Study Notes for Active and Passive Voice authored by the Google Gemini Academic Notes system.
• **Chapter Focus**: Comprehensive understanding, structural mechanics, tense transformations, and functional usage of the Passive Voice within the DAV school curriculum.
• **Voice Definition**: **Voice** is that form of a transitive verb which shows whether the subject of a sentence does the action or has the action done to it.
• **Active Voice Identification**: In the **Active Voice**, the subject of the sentence is the doer of the action, acting directly upon an object.
• **Passive Voice Identification**: In the **Passive Voice**, the subject of the sentence is the receiver or sufferer of the action rather than the doer.
• **Core Purpose of Passive Voice**: It is used when the focus is entirely on the action or the receiver of the action, rather than the person or thing performing the action.
• **Transitive Verb Requirement**: Only **transitive verbs** (verbs that take a direct object) can be changed from the Active Voice into the Passive Voice.
• **Intransitive Verb Limitation**: **Intransitive verbs** lack a direct object, and therefore, they cannot be converted into the Passive Voice.
• **Subject-Object Interchange**: The fundamental mechanical rule of voice transformation is that the **object** of the active verb becomes the **subject** of the passive verb.
• **Subject Demotion**: The original **subject** of the active sentence is demoted to become the object of a preposition (usually 'by') or is completely omitted in the passive structure.
• **Use of Preposition 'By'**: The preposition **'by'** is normally placed before the agent (the doer) in a passive sentence when the agent needs to be mentioned.
• **Verb Form Rule**: The main verb in any passive voice construction must *always* be converted into its **Past Participle (V3)** form.
• **Auxiliary Verb Requirement**: The Past Participle (V3) must always be preceded by an appropriate form of the auxiliary verb **'be'** (am, is, are, was, were, being, been).
• **Pronoun Case Changes**: Subjective pronouns used in the active voice must change to their corresponding **objective pronouns** when they move to the agent position in the passive voice.

• **Pronoun Transformation Map**: The pronoun **'I'** in the active voice changes to **'me'** in the passive agent phrase.
• **Pronoun Transformation Map**: The pronoun **'We'** in the active voice changes to **'us'** in the passive agent phrase.
• **Pronoun Transformation Map**: The pronoun **'He'** in the active voice changes to **'him'** in the passive agent phrase.
• **Pronoun Transformation Map**: The pronoun **'She'** in the active voice changes to **'her'** in the passive agent phrase.
• **Pronoun Transformation Map**: The pronoun **'They'** in the active voice changes to **'them'** in the passive agent phrase.
• **Pronoun Transformation Map**: The pronoun **'You'** remains unchanged as **'you'** when transitioning from active to passive voice.
• **Pronoun Transformation Map**: The pronoun **'It'** remains unchanged as **'it'** when transitioning from active to passive voice.
• **Tense Preservation Rule**: The tense of the original active verb must be strictly maintained and reflected through the auxiliary verb in the passive voice.
• **Overview of Tense Matrix**: Only **eight tenses** out of the twelve standard English tenses can be successfully converted into the passive voice.
• **Excluded Tenses**: The four tenses excluded from passive transformation are the Present Perfect Continuous, Past Perfect Continuous, Future Continuous, and Future Perfect Continuous.
• **Simple Present Tense Structure**: In the **Simple Present Tense**, the passive voice uses the auxiliary verbs **is / am / are** followed by the Past Participle (V3) of the main verb.
• **Simple Present Active Example**: Active: "The teacher **punishes** the naughty boy." -> Subject + V1/V5 + Object.
• **Simple Present Passive Example**: Passive: "The naughty boy **is punished** by the teacher." -> New Subject + is/am/are + V3 + by + Agent.
• **Plural Object Handling**: When the new subject in the Simple Present passive is plural, the auxiliary verb must change accordingly (e.g., "The books **are read** by the students").
• **Negative Simple Present**: In negative sentences, the auxiliary is followed by 'not' (e.g., "The letter **is not written** by her").

• **Present Continuous Tense Structure**: In the **Present Continuous Tense**, the passive voice uses the auxiliary structure **is / am / are + being** followed by the Past Participle (V3).
• **Present Continuous Action Indicator**: The addition of the word **'being'** is mandatory to show that the action is ongoing or continuous at the time of speaking.
• **Present Continuous Active Example**: Active: "She **is writing** a letter." -> Subject + is/am/are + V1-ing + Object.
• **Present Continuous Passive Example**: Passive: "A letter **is being written** by her." -> New Subject + is/am/are + being + V3 + by + Agent.
• **Plural Present Continuous Example**: When the object is plural, use 'are being' (e.g., "The cars **are being repaired** by the mechanic").
• **Simple Past Tense Structure**: In the **Simple Past Tense**, the passive voice uses the auxiliary verbs **was / were** followed by the Past Participle (V3) of the main verb.
• **Simple Past Tense Indicator**: **Was** is used for singular subjects, and **were** is used for plural subjects in the past passive structure.
• **Simple Past Active Example**: Active: "The hunter **killed** a tiger." -> Subject + V2 + Object.
• **Simple Past Passive Example**: Passive: "A tiger **was killed** by the hunter." -> New Subject + was/were + V3 + by + Agent.
• **Plural Simple Past Example**: Passive: "The tigers **were killed** by the hunter." -> Demonstrating subject-verb agreement in the past tense.
• **Negative Simple Past Example**: Active: "He did not invite me." transforms to Passive: "I **was not invited** by him."
• **Past Continuous Tense Structure**: In the **Past Continuous Tense**, the passive voice uses the auxiliary structure **was / were + being** followed by the Past Participle (V3).
• **Past Continuous Active Example**: Active: "They **were playing** a match." -> Subject + was/were + V1-ing + Object.
• **Past Continuous Passive Example**: Passive: "A match **was being played** by them." -> New Subject + was/were + being + V3 + by + Agent.
• **Plural Past Continuous Example**: Passive: "Matches **were being played** by them." -> Ensuring correct agreement for plural objects.

• **Present Perfect Tense Structure**: In the **Present Perfect Tense**, the passive voice uses the auxiliary structure **has / have + been** followed by the Past Participle (V3) of the main verb.
• **Present Perfect Agreement**: **Has been** is used for third-person singular subjects, while **have been** is used for first-person, second-person, and all plural subjects.
• **Present Perfect Active Example**: Active: "Rohan **has completed** his homework." -> Subject + has/have + V3 + Object.
• **Present Perfect Passive Example**: Passive: "His homework **has been completed** by Rohan." -> New Subject + has/have + been + V3 + by + Agent.
• **Plural Present Perfect Example**: Passive: "All the assignments **have been completed** by the students." -> Demonstrating plural auxiliary usage.
• **Past Perfect Tense Structure**: In the **Past Perfect Tense**, the passive voice uses the universal auxiliary structure **had + been** followed by the Past Participle (V3).
• **Past Perfect Uniformity**: Unlike present perfect, **had been** is used uniformly for all subjects regardless of whether they are singular or plural.
• **Past Perfect Active Example**: Active: "The police **had caught** the thief before he fled." -> Subject + had + V3 + Object.
• **Past Perfect Passive Example**: Passive: "The thief **had been caught** by the police before he fled." -> New Subject + had + been + V3 + by + Agent.
• **Future Simple Tense Structure**: In the **Simple Future Tense**, the passive voice uses the auxiliary structure **shall / will + be** followed by the Past Participle (V3).
• **Simple Future Agreement**: **Will be** is standard for most modern English structures, while **shall be** is traditionally used with first-person pronouns (I, we).
• **Simple Future Active Example**: Active: "The principal **will announce** the results tomorrow." -> Subject + shall/will + V1 + Object.
• **Simple Future Passive Example**: Passive: "The results **will be announced** by the principal tomorrow." -> New Subject + shall/will + be + V3 + by + Agent + Time.
• **Future Perfect Tense Structure**: In the **Future Perfect Tense**, the passive voice uses the auxiliary structure **shall / will + have + been** followed by the Past Participle (V3).
• **Future Perfect Active Example**: Active: "She **will have cooked** dinner by 8 PM." -> Subject + shall/will + have + V3 + Object.
• **Future Perfect Passive Example**: Passive: "Dinner **will have been cooked** by her by 8 PM." -> New Subject + shall/will + have + been + V3 + by + Agent + Time.

• **Interrogative Sentences Overview**: Transforming interrogative sentences (questions) into the passive voice requires careful handling of word order and auxiliary placement.
• **Yes/No Question Transformation**: Questions starting with auxiliary verbs (**Do, Does, Did, Is, Are, Has, Have**, etc.) retain their interrogative form in the passive voice.
• **Present Simple Interrogative Active**: Active: "**Does** she write a letter?" -> Auxiliary + Subject + V1 + Object?
• **Present Simple Interrogative Passive**: Passive: "**Is** a letter written by her?" -> New Auxiliary (Is/Am/Are) + New Subject + V3 + by + Agent?
• **Past Simple Interrogative Active**: Active: "**Did** he break the window?" -> Did + Subject + V1 + Object?
• **Past Simple Interrogative Passive**: Passive: "**Was** the window broken by him?" -> Was/Were + New Subject + V3 + by + Agent?
• **Present Continuous Interrogative**: Active: "**Are** they cleaning the room?" -> Passive: "**Is** the room **being cleaned** by them?"
• **Present Perfect Interrogative**: Active: "**Have** you finished the job?" -> Passive: "**Has** the job **been finished** by you?"
• **'Wh-' Word Questions Rule**: Questions beginning with **'Wh-' words** (Who, What, Where, When, Why, How) retain the question word at the beginning of the passive sentence.
• **Special Rule for 'Who'**: When an active question begins with **'Who'**, it transforms into **'By whom'** at the beginning of the passive sentence.
• **'Who' Active Example**: Active: "**Who** painted this wall?" -> Who + V2 + Object?
• **'Who' Passive Example**: Passive: "**By whom** was this wall painted?" -> By whom + was/were + New Subject + V3?
• **'What' or 'Which' Questions**: Questions starting with 'What' or 'Which' keep the word in place, followed by the correct passive auxiliary structure.
• **Imperative Sentences Definition**: **Imperative sentences** express commands, requests, advice, or suggestions, and they typically lack a stated subject (understood as 'you').
• **Imperative Passive Formula (Commands)**: Imperative sentences expressing a command are converted into the passive voice using the structure **Let + object + be + past participle (V3)**.

• **Command Active Example**: Active: "**Open** the door." -> Verb (V1) + Object.
• **Command Passive Example**: Passive: "**Let** the door **be opened**." -> Let + Object + be + V3.
• **Negative Command Structure**: Negative imperative commands starting with "Do not" are converted using the formula **Let + object + not + be + V3**.
• **Negative Command Example**: Active: "**Do not beat** the animal." -> Passive: "**Let** the animal **not be beaten**."
• **Advice and Suggestion Imperatives**: Imperative sentences that express moral duty, advice, or general suggestions are best transformed using the modal structure **should be**.
• **Advice Active Example**: Active: "**Help** the poor." -> Expressing moral obligation.
• **Advice Passive Example**: Passive: "The poor **should be helped**." -> New Subject + should + be + V3.
• **Respect Example**: Active: "**Respect** your elders." -> Passive: "Your elders **should be respected**."
• **Imperative Sentences with Requests**: Sentences beginning with "Please" or "Kindly" drop those words and are prefixed with the phrase **"You are requested to..."** in the passive voice.
• **Request Active Example**: Active: "**Please** lend me some money." -> Please + Verb + Object.
• **Request Passive Example**: Passive: "**You are requested to** lend me some money." -> You are requested to + base active clause.
• **Order and Command Framing**: Sentences expressing strict commands can also be framed using **"You are ordered to..."** followed by the active predicate.
• **Order Example**: Active: "**Leave** the room immediately!" -> Passive: "**You are ordered to** leave the room immediately."
• **Advice Framing Alternative**: General advice can alternatively be framed using **"You are advised to..."**.
• **Advice Framing Example**: Active: "**Take** your medicine on time." -> Passive: "**You are advised to** take your medicine on time."

• **Modals in Passive Voice**: Modal auxiliary verbs (**can, could, may, might, must, should, would, ought to**) follow a specific, uniform rule for passive transformation.
• **Modal Passive Formula**: The passive voice structure for modal verbs is **Modal + be + Past Participle (V3)**.
• **Can Active Example**: Active: "He **can lift** this heavy box." -> Subject + Modal (can) + V1 + Object.
• **Can Passive Example**: Passive: "This heavy box **can be lifted** by him." -> New Subject + modal (can) + be + V3 + by + Agent.
• **Must Active Example**: Active: "We **must obey** the traffic rules." -> Subject + must + V1 + Object.
• **Must Passive Example**: Passive: "The traffic rules **must be obeyed** by us." -> New Subject + must + be + V3 + by + Agent.
• **Could Active Example**: Active: "She **could solve** the puzzle easily." -> Passive: "The puzzle **could be solved** by her easily."
• **May Active Example**: Active: "The teacher **may grant** you leave." -> Passive: "You **may be granted** leave by the teacher."
• **Sentences with Two Objects**: Some transitive verbs (like *give, teach, offer, send, lend, promise*) take **two objects**: a **Direct Object** (usually a thing) and an **Indirect Object** (usually a person).
• **Dual Object Passive Rule**: Either the direct object or the indirect object can become the subject of the passive sentence, though using the **indirect object** (the person) is much more common.
• **Dual Object Active Example**: Active: "The teacher **gave** *me* a prize." -> Subject + V2 + Indirect Object (me) + Direct Object (a prize).
• **Indirect Object as Passive Subject**: Passive: "*I* **was given** a prize by the teacher." -> Using the person as the new subject.
• **Direct Object as Passive Subject**: Passive: "A prize **was given** *to me* by the teacher." -> Using the thing as the new subject, requiring the preposition 'to' before the indirect object.
• **Omission of Agent**: The agent (by + doer) is **omitted** in the passive voice when the doer is unknown, obvious from context, unimportant, or general (e.g., *people, someone, they, police*).
• **Omission Example**: Active: "**Someone** has stolen my pen." -> Passive: "My pen **has been stolen**." (Omitting "by someone" because it is redundant).

• **Prepositions with Passive Verbs**: While the preposition **'by'** is standard for most passive agents, certain verbs require specific, fixed prepositions instead of 'by'.
• **Verb 'Surprise' Preposition**: The verb **'surprise'** takes the preposition **'at'** in the passive voice.
• **Surprise Example**: Active: "His strange behavior **surprised** me." -> Passive: "I **was surprised at** his strange behavior." (Not 'by').
• **Verb 'Know' Preposition**: The verb **'know'** takes the preposition **'to'** in the passive voice.
• **Know Example**: Active: "Everyone **knows** him." -> Passive: "He **is known to** everyone." (Not 'by').
• **Verb 'Contain' Preposition**: The verb **'contain'** takes the preposition **'in'** in the passive voice.
• **Contain Example**: Active: "This box **contains** many secrets." -> Passive: "Many secrets **are contained in** this box."
• **Verb 'Interest' Preposition**: The verb **'interest'** takes the preposition **'in'** in the passive voice.
• **Interest Example**: Active: "This book **interests** me." -> Passive: "I **am interested in** this book."
• **Verb 'Alarm' Preposition**: The verb **'alarm'** takes the preposition **'at'** in the passive voice.
• **Alarm Example**: Active: "The loud noise **alarmed** us." -> Passive: "We **were alarmed at** the loud noise."
• **Verb 'Displease' Preposition**: The verb **'displeased'** takes the preposition **'with'** in the passive voice.
• **Displeased Example**: Active: "His rudeness **displeased** the manager." -> Passive: "The manager **was displeased with** his rudeness."
• **Verb 'Saturate' Preposition**: The verb **'saturate'** takes the preposition **'with'** in the passive voice.
• **Saturate Example**: Active: "Water **saturated** the soil." -> Passive: "The soil **was saturated with** water."
• **Prepositional Consistency**: Memorizing these fixed prepositional pairings is essential for scoring full marks in DAV English examinations and practice book exercises.

• **Passive Voice with Intransitive Prepositional Verbs**: An intransitive verb followed by a fixed preposition can sometimes act as a transitive unit and take a passive form.
• **Prepositional Verb Example**: Active: "The car **ran over** the dog." -> Verb + Preposition acting on an object.
• **Prepositional Verb Passive**: Passive: "The dog **was run over** by the car." -> Retaining the phrasal preposition intact before the agent.
• **Laugh At Example**: Active: "Do not **laugh at** the poor." -> Passive: "Let the poor **not be laughed at**."
• **Infinitives in Passive Voice**: Sentences containing **infinitives** (to + V1) follow a distinct structural pattern when converted into the passive voice.
• **Infinitive Active Structure**: Active sentences with infinitives typically follow the pattern: **Subject + verb + object + to + V1**.
• **Infinitive Passive Formula**: The passive conversion follows the pattern: **Subject + verb + object + to + be + V3**.
• **Infinitive Active Example**: Active: "It is time **to close** the shop." -> Subject + verb + complement + to + V1 + Object.
• **Infinitive Passive Example**: Passive: "It is time for the shop **to be closed**." -> Inserting 'for' before the object and changing 'to close' to 'to be closed'.
• **Another Infinitive Example**: Active: "She has **to finish** this DAV project." -> Passive: "This DAV project has **to be finished** by her."
• **Quasi-Passive Verbs (Active in Form, Passive in Meaning)**: Certain verbs are active in form but convey a passive meaning and require special treatment.
• **Quasi-Passive Example (Taste)**: Active: "Honey **tastes** sweet." -> Subject + verb + complement.
• **Quasi-Passive Conversion Rule**: Honey is sweet **when it is tasted** (expanding the compressed passive clause).
• **Quasi-Passive Example (Read)**: Active: "The book **reads** well." -> Passive equivalent: "The book is good **when it is read**."
• **Quasi-Passive Example (Build)**: Active: "The house **is building**." -> Passive meaning: "The house **is being built**."

• **DAV Chapter Summary**: The passive voice is a vital grammatical tool used to shift emphasis from the doer of an action to the receiver or the action itself.
• **Core Checklist 1 (Transitivity)**: Always verify that the sentence contains a **direct object** before attempting to convert it into the passive voice.
• **Core Checklist 2 (V3 Form)**: Ensure that the main verb is invariably converted into its **Past Participle (V3)** form in every single passive sentence.
• **Core Checklist 3 (Auxiliary 'Be')**: Confirm that the correct form of the verb **'be'** (am, is, are, was, were, being, been) matches the tense and number of the new subject.
• **Core Checklist 4 (Pronoun Shift)**: Double-check that all personal pronouns are correctly shifted from their subjective case to their objective case in the agent phrase.
• **Core Checklist 5 (Tense Consistency)**: Verify that the tense of the transformed sentence strictly mirrors the tense of the original active sentence without shifting timeframes.
• **Core Checklist 6 (Interrogative Order)**: Ensure that questions retain their question marks and correct interrogative word order after transformation.
• **Core Checklist 7 (Imperative Rules)**: Apply the correct imperative formula ("Let... be", "should be", or "You are requested/ordered to") based on the tone of the command or request.
• **Core Checklist 8 (Modal Structure)**: Remember that modal auxiliary verbs must always be followed immediately by **'be'** and a Past Participle (V3).
• **Core Checklist 9 (Prepositional Accuracy)**: Watch out for special DAV textbook verbs that require DAV-specific prepositions (at, to, in, with) instead of the standard 'by'.
• **Core Checklist 10 (Agent Omission)**: Recognize when an agent is general or obvious (like 'someone' or 'DAV students') and safely omit the 'by' phrase for natural style.
• **DAV Examination Tip**: Read instructions in the English Practice Book carefully to identify whether a passage requires transformation from active to passive or passive to active.
• **Final Mastery Goal**: Regular practice of these DAV Chapter 7 rules ensures absolute grammatical precision, enhanced writing skills, and flawless performance in school assessments.
• **End of DAV Academic Notes**: Exhaustive 10-page study guide for Class 7 English Practice Book Chapter 7: Passive Voice successfully concluded.
